scholarly_argument_maston_divine_human_a.quote_verbatim: as developed by Ben Sira, indicates that law observance brings life and that humans have the moral capacity to obey. scholarly_argument_maston_josephus_as_ev.pdf_source: [local-path] SHAL/04_Littérature_secondaire/03_Paul/Divine and Human Agency in Second Temple Judaism and Paul_ A -- Jason Maston -- 1, 1, 2010 -- Mohr Siebeck -- 9783161516405 -- 0b228a0486e4e7293480e4698717d4e1 -- Anna’s Archive.md
scholarly_argument_maston_josephus_as_ev.page: 10-13 (Introduction, sec. B: The Jewish Schools, Human Action, and Fate)
scholarly_argument_maston_josephus_as_ev.chapter: Introduction, B: The Jewish Schools, Human Action, and Fate
scholarly_argument_maston_josephus_as_ev.quote_verbatim: Josephus' texts indicate that the claim that Judaism maintained that salvation was always by grace (divine action) not obedience (human action) is not entirely accurate. Also, the assertion that no one discussed the issue of divine and human agency is contradicted by Josephus. ... Josephus plots the three schools along a single line. The Essenes and Sadducees correspond to the extremes, with the Pharisees representing something of a compromise.
scholarly_argument_maston_josephus_as_ev.context: Maston uses Josephus (J.W. 2.119-166; Ant. 13.171-173; 18.11-25) as the primary external witness against the post-Sanders consensus that 'divine and human agency' is a modern, anachronistic frame for reading Judaism. He marshals Boccaccini's observation: 'the major ancient historian of Jewish thought took exactly the problem of the relationship between human and divine agency as the criterion for identifying the Jewish schools of thought of his time.'

scholarly_argument_maston_free_will_and_.pdf_source: [local-path] SHAL/04_Littérature_secondaire/03_Paul/Divine and Human Agency in Second Temple Judaism and Paul_ A -- Jason Maston -- 1, 1, 2010 -- Mohr Siebeck -- 9783161516405 -- 0b228a0486e4e7293480e4698717d4e1 -- Anna’s Archive.md
scholarly_argument_maston_free_will_and_.chapter: Chapter 1: Obedience and the Law of Life in Sirach, sec. B (Creator-creation framework)
scholarly_argument_maston_free_will_and_.quote_verbatim: It is not the case that obedience is merely the response of the faithful human to God's prior grace. Nor is it the case that obedience is simply the means to maintaining a life already possessed. Rather, obedience is the means to attaining life and blessing. Ben Sira exhorts his students to observe the law because he thinks that this is the only means to life. His nomism has not collapsed into perverse legalism in which one arrogantly demands blessing from God, as Sanders rightly noted, but it remains the case that Ben Sira contends that life comes through keeping the law.
scholarly_argument_maston_free_will_and_.context: Maston's anti-Sanders reading of Sirach: against covenantal nomism, Ben Sira does not treat obedience as a response to prior grace but as the means to life itself. Humans have genuine moral capacity; the two ways are real alternatives.

scholarly_argument_maston_hodayot_and_di.pdf_source: [local-path] SHAL/04_Littérature_secondaire/03_Paul/Divine and Human Agency in Second Temple Judaism and Paul_ A -- Jason Maston -- 1, 1, 2010 -- Mohr Siebeck -- 9783161516405 -- 0b228a0486e4e7293480e4698717d4e1 -- Anna’s Archive.md
scholarly_argument_maston_hodayot_and_di.chapter: Introduction, C; expanded in Chapter 2: God's Gracious Acts of Deliverance in the Hodayot
scholarly_argument_maston_hodayot_and_di.quote_verbatim: These statements highlight the act of predestination, the giving of knowledge, and the purification of the sinner. Each is attributed to God and especially to his spirit as the means through which God resolves the human's problem. Salvation itself rests solely in the hands of God. Yet the human agent is not merely the passive receiver of these great deeds. The hymnists portray the divine acts as empowering. What emerges from the Hodayot is not a denial of human agency, but a restored human agent empowered and continuously sustained by a gracious divine agent.
scholarly_argument_maston_hodayot_and_di.context: Maston's summary of the Hodayot model: divine predestination, gift of knowledge, purification, Spirit-empowerment as the structure of the divine-human relationship — with human agency restored but never autonomous.

scholarly_argument_maston_predestination.pdf_source: [local-path] SHAL/04_Littérature_secondaire/03_Paul/Divine and Human Agency in Second Temple Judaism and Paul_ A -- Jason Maston -- 1, 1, 2010 -- Mohr Siebeck -- 9783161516405 -- 0b228a0486e4e7293480e4698717d4e1 -- Anna’s Archive.md
scholarly_argument_maston_predestination.chapter: Introduction, C: The Argument of This Study
scholarly_argument_maston_predestination.quote_verbatim: In sharp contrast to this perspective, the Hodayot stresses the role played by the divine agent. The Hodayot comes very close to Josephus' Essenes who attributed all things to God or fate. It constantly highlights the individual's sinfulness and frailty, and what emerges from the overwhelmingly depressive anthropology is a critique of the human as a creature. This pessimistic anthropology is equally matched by statements about the marvellous grace and mercy of God.
scholarly_argument_maston_predestination.context: Maston explicitly frames the Hodayot's anthropology as creaturely incapacity (material and moral), with divine predestination determining salvation. This is positioned as more deterministic than covenantal nomism.

scholarly_argument_maston_paul_s_critiqu.pdf_source: [local-path] SHAL/04_Littérature_secondaire/03_Paul/Divine and Human Agency in Second Temple Judaism and Paul_ A -- Jason Maston -- 1, 1, 2010 -- Mohr Siebeck -- 9783161516405 -- 0b228a0486e4e7293480e4698717d4e1 -- Anna’s Archive.md
scholarly_argument_maston_paul_s_critiqu.page: 139-140 (Chapter 3, sec. A.2: Sin's Takeover of Human Capacity)
scholarly_argument_maston_paul_s_critiqu.chapter: Chapter 3: Sin, the Spirit, and Human Obedience in Romans 7-8, sec. A.2
scholarly_argument_maston_paul_s_critiqu.quote_verbatim: Both are created with 'free will' and the capacity to obey; both are confronted with the 'law of life;' and both are left by God to determine their own destinies. Obedience to the law is the means to life, which while defined differently is the goal for both. Paul and Ben Sira are both dependent on Deuteronomy 30.15-20. These parallels suggest that Paul has something similar to Ben Sira's view in mind as he writes Romans 7.7-25. Against this optimistic analysis of human capacity, Paul argues that it fails to account for the radical nature of Sin (ἁμαρτία). ... Sin is a demonic-like being that invades the human realm, asserts its rule over the human, infects his flesh, and leads to his demise.
scholarly_argument_maston_paul_s_critiqu.context: Maston's central exegetical claim about Rom 7.7-25: Paul targets the Ben Sira / two-ways model and refutes its anthropology by introducing Sin as a malevolent indwelling power that destroys the very human agency the two-ways tradition presupposes.

scholarly_argument_maston_paul_s_critiqu.pdf_source: [local-path] SHAL/04_Littérature_secondaire/03_Paul/Divine and Human Agency in Second Temple Judaism and Paul_ A -- Jason Maston -- 1, 1, 2010 -- Mohr Siebeck -- 9783161516405 -- 0b228a0486e4e7293480e4698717d4e1 -- Anna’s Archive.md
scholarly_argument_maston_paul_s_critiqu.page: 139-140 (chapter 3 sec. A.2) and 170-172 (chapter 3, sec. C: Conclusion)
scholarly_argument_maston_paul_s_critiqu.chapter: Chapter 3, sec. A.2 (Sin's Takeover) and sec. C (Conclusion)
scholarly_argument_maston_paul_s_critiqu.quote_verbatim: In 7.7-25 he engages a Jewish view of law observance solely on Jewish premises (that is, he does not mention Christ except in a parenthetical comment [v.25]), and he disputes the claim that one can actually fulfil the law on anthropological grounds: because the human is a servant of Sin, he or she always does evil and will never attain to the life promised by the law. The argument is not nearly as convoluted as Sanders claimed when read against the backdrop of the two-ways tradition.
scholarly_argument_maston_paul_s_critiqu.context: Maston's broader synthesis: Rom 7:7-25 is an intra-Jewish critique of two-ways moral optimism on its own anthropological terms; Rom 8:1-13 then supplies the Christological-pneumatological resolution. The combined argument represents 'a radical reconfiguration of divine-human agency.'

scholarly_argument_maston_paul_s_adoptio.pdf_source: [local-path] SHAL/04_Littérature_secondaire/03_Paul/Divine and Human Agency in Second Temple Judaism and Paul_ A -- Jason Maston -- 1, 1, 2010 -- Mohr Siebeck -- 9783161516405 -- 0b228a0486e4e7293480e4698717d4e1 -- Anna’s Archive.md
scholarly_argument_maston_paul_s_adoptio.page: 156-157 and 169 (Chapter 3, sec. B: Obedience Accomplished through the Spirit)
scholarly_argument_maston_paul_s_adoptio.chapter: Chapter 3, sec. B (esp. B.2: The Establishment of Human Ability)
scholarly_argument_maston_paul_s_adoptio.quote_verbatim: Much like the Hodayot, Paul sets forth the Spirit as the divine agent who empowers the human to obey God's will. The Spirit is God's and Christ's presence in the intermediate time between Christ's ascension and his return. As the embodiment of the divine presence, the Spirit's task, according to 8.4-13, is to enable those 'in Christ' to please God by fulfilling the righteous requirement of the Torah. In this capacity, the Spirit creates human agency where Sin had prevented it.
scholarly_argument_maston_paul_s_adoptio.context: Maston's pivotal parallel: Paul in Rom 8.1-13 follows the structural logic of the Hodayot — Spirit as divine empowering agent — but with the decisive Christological modification (the Spirit must be the 'Spirit of Christ').

scholarly_argument_maston_christological.pdf_source: [local-path] SHAL/04_Littérature_secondaire/03_Paul/Divine and Human Agency in Second Temple Judaism and Paul_ A -- Jason Maston -- 1, 1, 2010 -- Mohr Siebeck -- 9783161516405 -- 0b228a0486e4e7293480e4698717d4e1 -- Anna’s Archive.md
scholarly_argument_maston_christological.chapter: Chapter 3, sec. B.1: The Christological Modification
scholarly_argument_maston_christological.quote_verbatim: Third, the linking of the Spirit with Christ not only signals a drastic redefinition of God, but also distinguishes Paul's conception of divine empowerment from his contemporaries. While other Jews pointed to the Spirit as the means to obedience, Paul insists that the Spirit must be connected with Christ. It is not enough to claim that the Spirit of God helps one. Rather, the Spirit that assists must be the Spirit of Christ. This Christological modification to the pattern of the divine-human relationship already found in the Hodayot is significant. Whereas in the Hodayot, God's acts of deliverance were attributed to the outworking in time of his mysterious will to elect some unto salvation, Paul claims that God has invaded time in his Son (cf. Gal 1.4; 4.4-6).
scholarly_argument_maston_christological.context: Maston's specification of how Paul differs from the Hodayot: not pre-temporal election but the Christ-event. Spirit qua 'Spirit of Christ' (Rom 8.9) is the redefined divine empowering agent.

scholarly_argument_maston_moral_responsi.pdf_source: [local-path] SHAL/04_Littérature_secondaire/03_Paul/Divine and Human Agency in Second Temple Judaism and Paul_ A -- Jason Maston -- 1, 1, 2010 -- Mohr Siebeck -- 9783161516405 -- 0b228a0486e4e7293480e4698717d4e1 -- Anna’s Archive.md
scholarly_argument_maston_moral_responsi.page: 169-170 (Chapter 3, sec. B: closing remarks before Conclusion)
scholarly_argument_maston_moral_responsi.chapter: Chapter 3, sec. B (closing on the Hodayot/Paul parallel)
scholarly_argument_maston_moral_responsi.quote_verbatim: The insistence by both the hymnist and Paul that those in their salvific communities lead lives pleasing to God does not collapse into 'works-righteousness.' Both do make eternal life contingent on the human agent's enactment of God's work in them. But neither author describes human activity as independent of divine action. ... Both hold that human action is the expression of the divine impartation of life, so that far from trying to earn life, the human is revealing the life already possessed.
scholarly_argument_maston_moral_responsi.context: Maston preserves a meaningful place for human action even in the most deterministic framework: in both Hodayot and Paul, human action is the expression of divine impartation; the question is the configuration of divine-human relationship, not 'free will vs. determinism' in modern philosophical terms.

scholarly_argument_maston_paul_and_liber.pdf_source: [local-path] SHAL/04_Littérature_secondaire/03_Paul/Divine and Human Agency in Second Temple Judaism and Paul_ A -- Jason Maston -- 1, 1, 2010 -- Mohr Siebeck -- 9783161516405 -- 0b228a0486e4e7293480e4698717d4e1 -- Anna’s Archive.md
scholarly_argument_maston_paul_and_liber.chapter: Chapter 3, sec. B.2: The Establishment of Human Ability
scholarly_argument_maston_paul_and_liber.quote_verbatim: Paul views the Spirit as the enabler who establishes human agency, so that the believer is neither a puppet moved at God's whim nor an independent agent capable of acting apart from the Spirit.
scholarly_argument_maston_paul_and_liber.context: Maston's most explicit anti-libertarian formulation for Paul. The term autexousios does not appear in the volume. Paul's framework is Spirit-creates-agency, not autonomous-self-determination. The argument node correctly captures: Paul does not use libertarian free will vocabulary or framework.

scholarly_argument_maston_paul_s_positio.pdf_source: [local-path] SHAL/04_Littérature_secondaire/03_Paul/Divine and Human Agency in Second Temple Judaism and Paul_ A -- Jason Maston -- 1, 1, 2010 -- Mohr Siebeck -- 9783161516405 -- 0b228a0486e4e7293480e4698717d4e1 -- Anna’s Archive.md
scholarly_argument_maston_paul_s_positio.page: 171-172 (Chapter 3, sec. C: Conclusion); cf. conclusion of the book ch. 4
scholarly_argument_maston_paul_s_positio.quote_verbatim: Paul actually has several points of agreement with this view. Both have a pessimistic anthropology, prioritise divine action, and claim that obedience is possible only through the empowering of the divine Spirit. Yet, Paul finds this option flawed because it lacks any reference to Jesus as the Messiah. Here Sanders' insistence that Paul rejected Judaism because it lacks Jesus as the Christ is entirely accurate. Divine action for Paul must be understood as the Christ-event, and while Paul has a doctrine of election, this too must be brought into conformity with God's action in Christ.
scholarly_argument_maston_paul_s_positio.context: Maston's core positioning thesis: Paul is not a maverick outsider but a participant in an intra-Jewish debate; what places him outside acceptable Jewish bounds is Christology, not anti-Jewish grace-vs-works polemic.
